verses.text: This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: "Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way."
"A voice of one calling in the wilderness, 'Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.'"
John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.
People went out to him from all of Jerusalem and the countryside of Judea. Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River.
John was clothed in camel's hair, with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey.
And he proclaimed: "After me will come One more powerful than I, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie.
I baptize you with water, but He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit."
In those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan.
As soon as Jesus came up out of the water, He saw the heavens breaking open and the Spirit descending on Him like a dove.
And a voice came from heaven: "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased."
At once the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness,
and He was there for forty days, being tempted by Satan. He was with the wild animals, and the angels ministered to Him.
After the arrest of John, Jesus went into Galilee and proclaimed the gospel of God.
"The time is fulfilled," He said, "and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!"
As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, He saw Simon and his brother Andrew. They were casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
"Come, follow Me," Jesus said, "and I will make you fishers of men."
And at once they left their nets and followed Him.
Going on a little farther, He saw James son of Zebedee and his brother John. They were in a boat, mending their nets.
Immediately Jesus called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and followed Him.
Then Jesus and His companions went to Capernaum, and right away Jesus entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and began to teach.
The people were astonished at His teaching, because He taught as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.
Suddenly a man with an unclean spirit cried out in the synagogue:
"What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us? I know who You are—the Holy One of God!"
But Jesus rebuked the spirit. "Be silent!" He said. "Come out of him!"
At this, the unclean spirit threw the man into convulsions and came out with a loud shriek.
All the people were amazed and began to ask one another, "What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey Him!"
And the news about Jesus spread quickly through the whole region of Galilee.
As soon as Jesus and His companions had left the synagogue, they went with James and John to the home of Simon and Andrew.
Simon's mother-in-law was sick in bed with a fever, and they promptly told Jesus about her.
So He went to her, took her by the hand, and helped her up. The fever left her, and she began to serve them.
That evening, after sunset, people brought to Jesus all the sick and demon-possessed,
and the whole town gathered at the door.
And He healed many who were ill with various diseases and drove out many demons. But He would not allow the demons to speak, because they knew who He was.
Early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went out to a solitary place to pray.
Simon and his companions went to look for Him,
and when they found Him, they said, "Everyone is looking for You!"
But Jesus answered, "Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come."
So He went throughout Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and driving out demons.
Then a leper came to Jesus, begging on his knees: "If You are willing, You can make me clean."
Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. "I am willing," He said. "Be clean!"
And immediately the leprosy left him, and the man was cleansed.
Jesus promptly sent him away with a stern warning:
"See that you don't tell anyone. But go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them."

But the man went out and openly began to proclaim and spread the news. Consequently, Jesus could no longer enter a town in plain view, but He stayed out in solitary places. Yet people came to Him from every quarter.

context.author: Traditionally John Mark, a companion of Peter, writing what early church sources describe as Peter's own eyewitness memories set down in Rome
context.genre: Narrative Gospel — the shortest and, most scholars agree, the earliest-written of the four, marked by a fast, breathless pace
context.audience: Likely Roman Christians, probably facing persecution, who needed confidence that Jesus is the powerful, suffering Son of God — Mark explains Jewish customs for readers who wouldn't already know them, a sign of a non-Jewish audience.
context.setting: Mark opens with no birth narrative at all — a deliberate choice, plunging straight into John the Baptist and Jesus' baptism. Capernaum, on the Sea of Galilee's northwest shore, quickly becomes the operational base for everything that follows in this chapter.
context.custom: Rabbis of this era typically taught by citing the chain of earlier teachers behind a given interpretation. Jesus notably doesn't — He teaches directly, in His own voice, which is exactly what the astonished crowd in the Capernaum synagogue immediately picks up on.
context.timelineImmediate: This is the opening chapter of the entire Gospel — Mark introduces Jesus already as an adult, baptized and driven into the wilderness, then moves immediately into public ministry with barely a pause for explanation.
context.timelineBible: Mark opens by directly quoting a combined text from Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3, presenting John the Baptist as the fulfillment of a specific, centuries-old prophetic expectation before Jesus even appears on the page.
context.sparkNotes: Mark opens with no birth story at all — straight to John the Baptist, Jesus' baptism, and a forty-day wilderness temptation, all within the first thirteen verses. The word "immediately" (euthys) appears constantly through this chapter and the rest of Mark — of its 59 total New Testament uses, the overwhelming majority are in Mark alone, giving the whole Gospel its breathless, urgent pace right from the start.

translation.meaning: Literally "good news" — the very first word of Mark's opening line, naming the entire book before a single event has happened.

occurrences.note: Mark uses this word more often relative to his Gospel's short length than any other Gospel writer — fitting, since he names his whole work by it in the very first verse.

translation.meaning: Mark's signature word, appearing constantly through this single chapter alone — it gives the whole Gospel its rapid, urgent pace.

occurrences.note: The overwhelming majority of this word's New Testament uses are packed into Mark's sixteen short chapters — more than any other Gospel by a wide margin.

translation.meaning: Can mean either "tempted" or "tested" — the same event functions as both an attack and a proof of character.
Rightful power and command — what set Jesus apart from the scribes, who typically taught by citing prior rabbis rather than speaking on their own authority.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's parallel account of John the Baptist's ministry and Jesus' baptism.
Luke's version of the Capernaum synagogue exorcism and the healings at Simon's house.
John's account of the Baptist's testimony, told from a different angle entirely.

otBackground.note: The promised messenger preparing the way — quoted directly in v.2.
"A voice calling in the wilderness" — quoted directly in v.3, identifying John's role.
Elijah's rough, hairy garment — the model behind John's own camel-hair clothing, hinting he's the promised Elijah-like forerunner.

commentary.note: Gill draws out the significance of Jesus physically touching the leper in v.41 — under the Law, touching a leper made a person ceremonially unclean, and no ordinary person would have risked it. Gill reads Jesus' willingness to do so anyway as showing His purity working outward to cleanse, rather than the leper's uncleanness working inward to defile Him — the opposite direction the Law assumed contact would run.

Henry points out that unlike Matthew and Luke, Mark skips the nativity entirely and opens with John's ministry — treating this, not the birth, as the actual "beginning of the gospel." He observes that the chapter's two Old Testament quotations, from Malachi and Isaiah, were written roughly three centuries apart yet both point to this exact same moment. He also notes that John's austere, self-denying way of living was itself an early expression of the gospel spirit, well before he preached a single word.

JFB highlights Mark's characteristic abruptness — skipping everything that came before to plunge straight into John's ministry, as if impatient to reach Jesus's public life. They make an interesting observation: despite being the shortest of the four Gospels overall, Mark is often the fullest and most detailed in the specific scenes it does choose to include.
